The other thing that could be going on is packet shaping at the ISP. Packet shaping is when certain kinds of traffic are prioritized as being more important than other traffic. This can, for example, keep web browsing and direct downloads pretty fast while making games and other activities slow, or possibly have bad latency.

A way to test this is to use this online tool. It requires Java, and takes about 10 minutes to complete. If an ISP is going to shape your traffic at all, they'll probably do it to the bittorrent protocol so it's a good protocol to test.

This is one of the better possibilities, and there is one usually foolproof way around it: VPN. When using a VPN, all traffic looks the same to the ISP (it's encrypted), so they don't know what the packets are for and can't reliably downgrade gaming packets.

@jett__gaming, before you buy any new hardware try a VPN. You could try a free VPN such as VPN Book (use OpenVPN if possible), or pay for a single month to test a better VPN service, but I wouldn't be surprised if it helped.

No no no. There isn't 1 single packetloss. The line itself may have NO packetloss but the servers you are ROUTED thru may. The internet is a network of networks. You can get packetloss on 1 server on 1 ISP but not on another. Are you sure you are actually pinging the game server and not some other server, check that first.

If it is not packet loss, then it is jitters. You don't have a consistent ping. You need to look at EVERY ping result and not the average and see if there are any delays. You may also need to write your own script as the PING that uses UDP/TCP and hits the game server. As the normal ping utilities use ICMP and the routers may intentionally favor (not drop and not back-queue) ICMP requests.

I would do this. See if there is a ping command in your game. For example, if it is TF2, open the console and type 'status' to get your ping. Do this many times and see if it ever spikes. That will get your a true ping test to THAT server. Keep in mind, because of peering, some servers may work well on a given ISP and others don't. Check out the developer boards for that game and see if they have in-game ping and packetloss utils. You need good metrics to analyze this problem, I am 100% sure of that. Your ISP(s) are going to deny any problems of course. But if you can scientifically prove it, you can write a blog post about it and then they may actually fix it if you go public.

The internet is a network of networks, there is no single packetloss/jitter rate. It varies on every network you pass through and ISP effects which networks you are routed to. An ISP may be cheap and may have shitty routing tables (bad network engineers) or shitty peering agreements.

tl;dr: It's most likely that the Fiber ISP has bad routing tables, or bad peering agreements, or connects to a different internet back bone (as a result of bad routing tables).
